Published: 18:46 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:51 EST, 24 November 2026

Hibernian ended their long wait for a Premiership home win after overcoming Dundee in a hard-fought contest at Easter Road.

Martin Boyle and Nicky Cadden – who curled home a stunning effort from outside the box – had the hosts in command before the interval.

But Dundee, still licking their wounds after an 8-0 savaging at the hands of Hearts on Saturday, showed plenty of fight after the break and pulled one back through Joe Wright.

The visitors tried in vain to grab an equaliser and it was Hibs who were left satisfied by their first three points at home since beating Kilmarnock on April 4.

Manager Marink Reedijk was thrilled to have bounced back from their 4-0 weekend home defeat at the hands of Dundee United, saying: ‘I think it’s a good reaction to what we have done against Dundee United.

‘It’s important that you get the three points at home. Again, that’s a big win. I saw a front foot team again, I saw togetherness again, I saw a team who fought for every ball.

Martin Boyle takes the acclaim after scoring the all-important second goal for Hibernian

‘That’s not easy, they have to be patient, you have to be secure, you have to wait for your moment and we took these moments and that was really good to see.

‘The goal of Nicky [Cadden] is one to, we say, put in a frame and put on your wall as a painting. The one of Martin [Boyle] is why Martin is so important for us. He can disrupt an opponent if they are so organised and so close to each other and so deep.

‘As long as we keep ourselves, I think these are good signs.’

Hibs played on the front foot as they looked to start repairing the damage from the weekend. On a rare start, Togo international Thibault Klidje was lively and saw a header crash into the side-netting before hitting a harmless snap-shot straight at Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman.

From a short corner routine Hibs worked space for Cadden on the edge of the box from Josh Mulligan’s lay-off and his driving effort whistled just past a post.

Dundee were desperate to keep it tight at the back but offered little going forward. Just when it looked like they were beginning to settle Hibs hit them with two goals in three minutes before the break.

The first came in the 40th minute when Boyle fired a penalty past Goodman after being tripped by Ryan Finnigan.

Nicky Cadden unleashes an absolute pearler into the top corner to put Hibs in front

Cadden then found the top corner with a sublime curling effort from his left foot just outside the box. It was another short corner routine that saw Miguel Chaiwa set up the wing-back.

Despite the hammer blow of losing two goals in quick succession before the break, Dundee demonstrated at the start of the second half that they were not going to roll over.

Steven Pressley’s side upped their intensity as they searched for a goal to get themselves back in the game and that arrived in the 67th minute courtesy of Wright.

Substitute Callum Jones’ free-kick should have been put away by Ryan Astley but the ball broke back to Wright and he slammed the ball high into the net from six yards.

That set up a tense finish but Hibs desperately held on for a rare home victory.

For Pressley, who changed half of his outfield XI following his side’s weekend humiliation, there were also positives to take.

The Dark Blues boss said: ‘We’re disappointed to not come away with anything and to obviously lose the game. But I also thought we restored some degree of pride tonight.

‘Going into half-time 2-0 down, losing two late goals in the half, can be a little bit demoralising, especially for a team that has a bit of fragility on the back of the weekend’s result.

‘I thought we responded brilliantly. We showed a lot of courage, a lot of determination, a lot of spirit and, as I’ve said, I think we certainly restored some level of pride that allows us a foundation to move into the weekend.’

#1081. What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark without Russia.

Since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada said.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1075. The eight players that should be on Man United's January list to turn season around - even with paltry £50m budget: From a goalscorer available for just £7m to star desperate to reunite with Mauricio Pochettino and a flying left back

Published: 21:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 24 November 2026

Inside the corridors of power at Manchester United, there is not the same appetite for a January splurge as there is among the club's fanbase.

While the winter transfer window brings hope for supporters desperate to see the mistakes of the summer rectified, United's decision-makers are anticipating a far more modest outlay.

As exclusively revealed by Daily Mail Sport, United plan to spend less than £50million, with two additions targeted, one of which could be on loan.

Should United, currently 19th, remain in the bottom three by the time the window opens on January 1, there is a slim chance they go big in a desperate bid to guarantee their Premier League status.

But for now, the watchword inside United is discipline, and that means any recruitment will have to be more creative than ever before.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at the transfer landscape and assesses eight players – a mix of Premier League proven and some lesser-known quantities – who could fit United’s needs AND their budget…

Mauricio Pochettino needs recruits in January - although Man United's budget being below £50m won't help his cause

Brentford centre back Nathan Collins is one of United's top targets, but he won't be available on the cheap

Position: Centre back, Age: 25, Club: Brentford

Signing Premier League proven players is absolutely the preference of the United hierarchy, as evidenced by their recent business. Six of their past eight arrivals joined with experience in the division under their belt.

Collins is one of the club’s top targets for the winter window. The 25-year-old Brentford captain would bring leadership, an aerial presence and is comfortable as a ball carrier from the back, which Pochettino values.

Collins is seen as having many of the same attributes that Harry Maguire has brought to United over the years. And while he is not a flash name, he is viewed as a player that can immediately deliver some solidity.

Highly durable and a threat at set-pieces, Brentford won’t be willing to part with their captain, who is under contract until 2029, on the cheap.

Signing Collins would eat up most of the budget – but United are not deterred.

Position: Left back, Age: 25, Club: Man City

United made a late play to land the Algerian on loan in January, only for City to tell them they would only sanction a permanent exit. In the end, time ran out and Ait-Nouri stayed put.

He has started just one game in all competitions under Enzo Maresca and is yet to feature at all in the Premier League this season. His situation is unlikely to improve in the near future, either.

A loan with an obligation to buy could suit all parties here, even if sending Ait-Nouri to their fiercest rivals may be difficult for City to stomach.

Rayan Ait-Nouri (right) has fallen out of favour under Enzo Maresca and is yet to play a minute in the Premier League this season. Could he make a move across Manchester?

Position: Left back, Age: 27, Club: Crystal Palace

An intriguing option given United have been keeping tabs on Mitchell for over a year.

Palace are quite secretive when it comes to Mitchell – they kept his last contract extension under wraps – but as it stands, his deal is set to expire at the end of the season.

Mitchell has the stamina to cope with Pochettino’s style of play and what he lacks in end product, he makes up for with his relentless pressing and recovery pace. The same is true of Fulham's Calvin Bassey, but sources are increasingly sceptical about United's chances of signing him in January.

For all of Palace’s struggles, Mitchell is proven at this level and would likely hit the ground running. The fact United are not his only suitor is a sign they aren’t straying down a blind alley.

With the 27-year-old’s contract yet to be extended and big clubs sniffing around, he could prove to be this January’s Marc Guehi should United nip in ahead of Liverpool, with Reds boss Andoni Iraola also keen.

Tyrick Mitchell has the stamina to cope with Pochettino’s style of play and what he lacks in end product, he makes up for with his relentless pressing and recovery pace

Position: Forward, Age: 29, Club: Tottenham

Out of favour under Roberto De Zerbi, Richarlison could help Tottenham Hotspur, Manchester United and himself in one fell swoop.

In the summer, Spurs were looking for £20m for the Brazilian. Now the feeling is they would take a figure below £10m – some sources think £7m may suffice – to move on a player who has been kicking his heels since playing for the Under 21s away to Cheltenham Town in October.

Richarlison saw summer offers from Everton, Trabzonspor and Vasco da Gama fall through for various reasons and with United desperate to bolster their front line, this one could suit all parties. Richarlison is a strong presser from the front, versatile and better in the air than he is perhaps given credit for. He’s also no stranger to football's dark arts, something Pochettino appreciates.

The 29-year-old would offer a greater goal threat than Joshua Zirkzee, who saw moves of his own collapse in the summer, and showed last season what a threat he can be, scoring 11 league goals.

Spurs just want him out of the building and while that is normally a red flag, United need all the help they can get in a difficult market.

Richarlison is available for a bargain fee in January - even if he comes with some red flags attached

Position: Centre back, Age: 28, Club: AC Milan

United have rarely gone to the continent for recruits in recent seasons. But their limited budget makes Premier League players extremely difficult to acquire.

One option who might be available for a bargain fee is AC Milan's Fikayo Tomori, who is out of contract in the summer. The expectation in Milan is that Tomori will be moved on in January, allowing former United boss Ruben Amorim to add to his defence.

Tomori was initally frozen out by Amorim – he’d have a good ice-breaker should he pitch up at United! – and was even stripped of a squad number, before he was gradually reintroduced.

The England international has started just four games this season – only two in the league – and while Tomori has limitations in the air, he would bring Premier League experience and a level of leadership that is sorely lacking. His ability to bring the ball out and into midfield would make him a regular starter in Manchester.

When Milan won Serie A in 2022, Tomori was aggressive in his press and showed he could play on either side as a centre back, and also slot in at right back when required.

Milan want to sell him, United need defensive reinforcements, and a cut-price deal suits everyone. This one is a no-brainer, thanks to Amorim of all people.

Fikayo Tomori looks set to move on from AC Milan in January with former United boss Ruben Amorim keen to shuffle his defensive pack

Position: Left back/centre back, Age: 29, Club: Stuttgart

An experienced option that could cover multiple positions across the back line, Mittelstadt would prove really shrewd business.

Under contract until 2028, the player has not agitated for a move but sources in Germany have indicated no extension talks are underway at this stage.

Stuttgart are eighth in the Bundesliga and should European football start to look out of reach, a sale of someone like Mittelstadt may become a necessity.

United should look at him even though his resale value would be limited, as he would immediately bring experience and quality. Mittelstadt, who was Germany's first-choice left back at Euro 2024, is a proactive defender that doesn’t shirk challenges and his durability means United could count on him from the off – important given their lack of high-quality options at left back.

Signing Mittelstadt would go against everything the club's executives want to do – but they showed by bringing in the 29-year-old Youri Tielemans in the summer that they are prepared to make exceptions on some older players.

#1071. THE BREAKDOWN: How Florian Wirtz suddenly became the most powerful creative force in the Premier League - from Andoni Iraola's perfect tactics to Liverpool's Bradley Barcola effect

Published: 21:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 24 November 2026

After Florian Wirtz trudged off the field just over an hour into Liverpool’s defeat by Manchester City in October, sacrificed following Ryan Gravenberch’s red card, Jamie Carragher had once again seen enough of the £116million man.

‘I think he needs to come out of the team,’ said Carragher post-match. ‘I said that last time out and I'm going to say it again.’

Fast forward six weeks, and Wirtz was running the show for Liverpool as they put four past Manchester United in poor Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge, topping a stellar performance off with a goal and an assist. Carragher hailed the German’s stunning first-half volley as ‘a goal Dennis Bergkamp would have scored’.

How things change. This was a performance, even against an abysmal 10-man United, that showed Wirtz was ready, at last, to seize the big occasions.

Because, for so long, he wasn’t ready. Carragher was not alone in his earlier assessment, one shared by countless frustrated Liverpool fans. There was a feeling that this slight, wispy technician had the tools to flourish in the slower-paced Bundesliga, or even for Liverpool in the Champions League, but would, perhaps, remain unable to shine amid the rough and tumble of the Premier League.

Wirtz managed five goals and four assists in the Premier League last season and added only one assist this term before that City game. Since then, he’s come to life. Four assists and a couple of goals in the league with another one of each in the Champions League, a tally he will hope to add to on Wednesday evening against Club Bruges.

Florian Wirtz has suddenly sprung to life as a Liverpool player and is making his critics eat their words

Wirtz scores a majestic flick against Manchester United on Sunday

Since that City defeat, Wirtz is getting into dangerous positions more often. He is having more touches in the opposition box, more shots in the opposition box, playing more passes into the opposition box and creating more than twice as many chances from open play.

Wirtz boasts a league-high 29 of those this season, and 20 of the chances have come since that City game.

The last player to create more than the 10 open-play chances Wirtz managed against United was David Silva in 2015. Wirtz created nine against Brentford, too, in the first league match after the City defeat, meaning he’s the only Premier League player on record (since 2003-04) to create nine or more chances from open play in multiple games in the same season. Wirtz did it twice in five weeks.

Let’s nip this one in the bud early. It is clear, of course, that Jurgen Klopp, the legendary former Liverpool manager now Germany head coach, has got a tune out of Wirtz in recent months. The pair, according to those who follow the national team, are very close.

‘Wirtz is a once-in-a-century talent,’ was Klopp’s assessment last year, while he later remarked that he was ‘shocked’ by how good Wirtz was in their first training session together.

The 23-year-old has shown it in matches, too, with four goals and an assist in his last four games for Germany, including a brace last week against the Netherlands.

This has fed a narrative of how Klopp has been the one to unlock Wirtz’s powers. Klopp deserves credit, naturally, but he is also helped by having the freedom to give Wirtz what he needs: space.

‘What do I need to be at my best? Ideally, a lot of space in every game so I can do what I want!’ said Wirtz after scoring one and setting up the other in Germany’s 2-0 win over Serbia in October.

He was half-joking, laughing as he said it, but he’s right. Technical creators like Wirtz thrive on space. He’s been able to have more of that in international football, with Klopp even playing him as a false nine to give him all the creative freedom he needs. He leads the press but the midfielders behind him do the bulk of the dirty work to allow Wirtz, the star, to shine.

Wirtz’s performances with his country have helped grow his confidence, but it would be deeply unfair on Iraola to suggest Klopp’s blueprint is the one now being copied.

Even if Liverpool and Germany play a similar style, it is much, much harder to give players freedom in the Premier League.

But if anyone was going to find a way to do it for Wirtz, it was Iraola.

Arne Slot could never work it out. By the end of his tenure, he’d played Wirtz as an attacking midfielder, stuck him on both flanks and thrust him up front. It was a conundrum he just couldn’t solve.

Iraola's Bournemouth side were one of the hardest-working, highest-pressing teams in the division but his system was still able to allow the likes of Justin Kluivert or Junior Kroupi to create and drift into pockets of space to set the attacking tempo.

For Iraola, it was always going to be Wirtz. The German has started every league game, all of them in the No 10 position.

He’s always led the way off the ball – only three players have won possession more often in the final third this season – but Iraola has been finding different ways to get the best out of him with the ball, too. Against Brentford, he shifted Rio Ngumoha inside almost to play as a second No 10 beside Wirtz, which helped create space for him to set up Liverpool's equaliser.

Having Alexis Mac Allister behind him allows Wirtz to concentrate on being the creative heartbeat, while even Dominik Szoboszlai has played noticeably deeper since returning from injury.

Andoni Iraola has started Wirtz in every league game, all of them in the No 10 position

Szoboszlai isn't the only one. Another aspect of Germany's game that has helped Wirtz is lining up alongside strikers who like to drop deep in Kai Havertz and Nick Woltemade, leaving space for Wirtz to attack.

In recent weeks, especially against United, Liverpool striker Alexander Isak has been doing the same. It was Isak doing exactly that which led to Wirtz’s goal.

Isak (below, in possession) drops in, plays the ball out wide to Ngumoha and Wirtz sprints into the box to get on to the end of the cross.

Alexander Isak dropped into midfield and sprayed the ball wide to Rio Ngumoha before Wirtz's goal against United

Isak missed much of last season through injury but his all-round play is much better attuned to Wirtz's game than those who played alongside him for most of 2025-26, including Hugo Ekitike.

One of the most devastating aspects of Iraola’s Bournemouth was how quickly players flooded forward when they attacked.

His Liverpool side is starting to do the same which, in turn, helps get the best out of Wirtz.

Last season under Slot, the likes of Cody Gakpo and Mo Salah would often tuck in instead of bombing forward out wide and Milos Kerkez, one of the most attacking full backs in the division under Iraola at Bournemouth, rarely did the same under Slot.

Now, Liverpool’s wingers are flying. This season under Iraola, Liverpool are averaging more ‘fast breaks’, how Opta define counter attacks, and shots from them than in any campaign under Slot or even the ‘heavy metal’ Klopp.

Wirtz has attempted seven through balls this season, one of the highest tallies in the division. Since the City game in particular, he has tried to play passes with purpose into the box.

Wirtz was creating chances in the first six games of this season but only a few of them were penetrating passes into the box

The German's chances created in the last five games, since the City defeat, show how many balls he is playing into dangerous areas

The rapid Bradley Barcola starting to find his feet since his £123m move has been a huge help to Wirtz.

Of Wirtz’s 20 open-play chances created since the City game, a quarter of them have been for Barcola.

Having those runners out wide like Barcola and Ngumoha is so helpful for the German. As he drives forward with the ball against United (below), he has three runners ahead of him with even Szoboszlai bursting forward. Wirtz has so many options and eventually slips in Isak for a great chance.

Liverpool had wide runners driving forward against United, helping Wirtz create chances and split their defence

You can see from the average position map from the game (below), just how attacking Liverpool’s wingers – and Kerkez – were, albeit, granted, against 10 men for most of the contest.

The average position map of Liverpool's players against United shows how high up the pitch they played

Wirtz has had a run like this before, around this time last year. During December and January, he racked up four league goals and three assists – having not managed a single one until then – only to notch one of each for the rest of the Premier League campaign.

You get the sense, though, with his confidence growing under managers for both club and country who want to play his way, that he might just keep shining this time.

#1069. BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–15 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

On 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, says Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

The BepiColumbo spacecraft (illustration).Credit: ESA - P. Carril

Travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo launched in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.

#1068. Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

Arteta became increasingly irate in the first few minutes after the restart, with Ben White on the receiving end of one verbal slap. Rice also received a telling-off, and a yellow card, from the referee after kicking the ball away in annoyance.

Would Slavia have secured a draw if they had been at full strength? They had been weakened by the banishment of their star striker from the club because of a series of disciplinary failings. Tomás Chory, the top scorer for the past two seasons, was chucked out of the team after showing his middle finger to the referee in a recent game. This sort of sanction would have earned Arteta’s approval, no doubt, but it did not increase Slavia’s chances of hurting the Premier League champions in those edgy final few minutes.

Perhaps they will reflect on that decision differently now, given the uncharacteristically wobbly second-half performance by Arsenal. The visitors were vulnerable in the latter stages, when they lacked the control and composure that Arteta expects. Gabriel, too, appeared dismayed by what he was seeing. At one point, he put his hands on his hips and scowled at his team-mates like an angry teacher.

With only a few minutes remaining, Nowak converted a left-wing cross to plunge Arsenal into a proper panic. It required a backs-to-the-wall defensive action, similar to the victory against Liverpool on Sunday, to get over the line.

Always we need to value winning away in the Champions League. It is extremely difficult. Two very different halves. We should have had three or four goals in the first half but we didn’t do it. Right at the start of the second half we were on the back foot, very sloppy and gave balls away. Then we had to suffer. A lot to learn.

We should have scored more in the first half and if we didn’t do that we had to go and do that in the second half.

We made six changes but we know the quality of the players we have. Whether we were lacking something I don’t know but I would have done the same thing [again].

I value what the team has done now, it is 11 away games we played, but our standards should be higher.

Arteta on Gyokeres: "He was really good. A game we believed was good for him, for the spaces he could use. He was really connected to the team. Great news because I think he needed that. Really pleased."

Arteta: "Two very different halves. The first we played at a really high level. At half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning we were extremely far from our standards. Very far from the standards we expect from each other."

First half we played really, really well. We created a lot of chances and could have scored more but the second half was completely different. They stepped up a gear and made it difficult for us and we have to learn from it. Delighted with the win but a lot of things to improve going forward.

Maybe they started pressing a bit higher with more intensity. We had too many giveaways especially in the final third. There was too much running from box to box and we have to manage those reactions and go for the third and fourth goal.

At the end of the day it is three points.

Slavia Prague managed just one shot on goal in the first half worth 0.12 xG but finished the game with 18 shots on Arsenal’s goal and 2.23 xG. Arsenal could easily have dropped points on the balance of the second 45 minutes.

Quite surprised Declan Rice stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes there. He seemed to be in a bit of discomfort after a couple of long sprints. And then he got the silly yellow. Arteta perhaps panicking about the result.

Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

On that occasion last year, Max Dowman became the youngest player in Champions League history. He should get more minutes tonight from the bench, given that he is currently suspended from Premier League action following his controversial red card against Fleetwood last week.

That’s the most Arteta has rotated between a Premier League and Champions League game so far this season. Telling perhaps that Konsa, Gabriel and Rice – the team’s defensive bedrock – stay in place. But changes on both sides at full-back, and in the attacking midfield areas.

Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#1062. Trinity Rodman pulls out of USA roster for upcoming tournament just hours after shock split from Ben Shelton

By JAKE FENNER, US SPORTS WRITER and DAN MATTHEWS

Published: 22:24 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 01:41 EST, 25 November 2026

United States women's soccer star Trinity Rodman has backed out of an upcoming tournament hours after reports revealed she is no longer in a relationship with tennis star Ben Shelton.

Rodman was set to take part in the 2026 CONCACAF W Championship window in Texas, but has now pulled out due to what US Soccer called 'a minor shoulder injury' in a statement announcing the roster move.

The statement says the injury occurred during the 2026 NWSL Championship Game last Saturday, where Rodman and the Washington Spirit fell 2-1 to the Kansas City Current. US Soccer has replaced Rodman with Gotham FC winger Jaedyn Shaw.

Rodman's removal comes hours after the Daily Mail was first to report on her split from the American tennis star.

The American sporting couple began dating around March 2025, frequently supporting one another at their various events, but have recently decided to call time on their relationship.

Their conflicting work schedules and constant travel made it too challenging for the couple to continue maintaining their relationship, the Daily Mail understands. However, the pair are believed to remain close, despite their split.

American soccer stat Trinity Rodman has backed out of the USWNT roster for the 2026 CONCACAF W Championship taking place beginning later this week

The announcement comes hours after the Daily Mail was first to report her split from longtime boyfriend and tennis star Ben Shelton

US Soccer says Rodman suffered 'a minor shoulder injury' in the 2026 NWSL Championship

The couple were frequently forced to maintain their romance over long distance with Shelton constantly traveling around the globe while playing on the ATP Tour.

Despite multiple sacrifices and last-minute trips to attend each other's matches, it appears they could no longer make it work.

The Daily Mail has reached out to both Shelton and Rodman's representatives for comment.

Shelton, 24, suffered defeat in the semi-final of the ATP Finals on Saturday, losing 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) to Carlos Alcaraz in Turin, Italy.

The same evening, Rodman, 24, and the Washington Spirit lost the NWSL final to the KC Current.

The following evening, the American tennis star was spotted at Madison Square Garden for the New York Knicks' game against the Indiana Pacers without Rodman, instead sitting on Celebrity Row alongside a friend and actress Inde Navarette.

The couple first went public with their relationship in March 2025 following speculation from fans.

Mystery surrounded the early stages of their relationship, as they initially dropped a playful hint as part of a TikTok trend last March then 'hard launched' their romance soon afterwards.

Their conflicting work schedules made it too challenging to maintain their relationship

Rodman was a near-permanent fixture in Shelton's box throughout the US Open in September.

The USWNT star and the Spirit had played an NWSL game in Washington on the day of the final but Rodman left the capital almost immediately after the final whistle to make the mad dash to New York for Shelton's final.

#1059. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#1057. RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: The grubby antics of JJ Gabriel's entourage threaten to derail his career before it's begun. Man United insiders tell a revealing story about his acrimonious exit

Published: 21:01 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 06:42 EST, 21 November 2026

We should start with the video. It’s something to behold. Opening with a scene that depicts a young footballer being ushered through a crowd of faux reporters, there is a promise within the first five seconds of ‘epic news’ and ‘a rare discovery’.

It’s a little on-the-nose, but the messaging will only escalate. Soon we find ourselves staring at what appears to be a Ballon d’Or replica, before the director cuts to a moody shot of the footballer from behind as he stares at a wall of photographs.

Those images are showing a few of the staging posts in his brief career to date – signing for Manchester United aged 10, posing with a ball and, then, one of him preparing to come on as a substitute. A pair of Nike boots find their way in.

Finally, the lad shows himself and delivers a single line to camera: ‘I am epic.’

This came out at the start of the week. Our epic footballer? That would be JJ Gabriel, aged 16 years and one month, still in braces, and potentially the best you’ve not yet seen.

As you have likely heard, he really is that good. And as you will also know, the mechanisms of his exit from United ahead of an imminent deal with Real Madrid have been ugly.

JJ Gabriel, aged 16 years and one month, still in braces, and potentially the best footballer you’ve not yet seen

The video Gabriel released this week announcing his exit from Manchester United includes signing for the club at the age of 10 alongside Cristiano Ronaldo Jr (Source: Instagram/Jjnr10)

Finally, the lad shows himself and delivers a single line to camera: ‘I am epic’ (Source: Instagram/Jjnr10)

But let’s momentarily keep to that bizarre video, which has been watched almost two million times on Gabriel’s Instagram page, and from there we can raise the question of whoever thought it was a good idea.

This is where we should introduce Ali Barat, the owner of Epic Sports. He’s a big fish in the world of football agencies and the 31-second clip was advertising their latest coup: Gabriel had joined his group, which is timely because a move to Real is imminent and that will follow other big deals brokered by Barat.

They include Moises Caicedo to Chelsea for £115million, Noni Madueke to Arsenal for £52m and Dean Huijsen to Bournemouth for £12.6m, then on to Real Madrid for £50m more. He’s a significant figure with a changeable definition of what it means to be understated. Here’s an example from his company’s website: ‘While some agents seek the spotlight, Ali Barat is quietly reshaping the transfer market.’

Amusingly, it then goes on to describe Barat as a ‘super-agent’ twice in the same paragraph while declaring he is ‘not just closing deals, he is building careers, guiding legacies, and setting the standard for a new era of football representation’.

The ‘quiet’ part was possibly lost along the way. But ‘legacy’ is the word among that salad most worthy of fixation, because Gabriel has been steered to a series of pivotal decisions at an incredibly young age.

He is yet to play a single minute of competitive senior football but he is clear on what he wishes to become. Earlier this month, his handlers felt it prudent to place him in an interview with the Madrid-based newspaper Marca and Gabriel said: ‘My dream is to win a Ballon d'Or.’

Fair enough. He’s a teenager aiming high. Is it wise to say so? Maybe not, but he’s 16. Barat, the super-agent, has no such excuse. He’s 30 years older than his client and saw no harm in a video that invoked the Ballon d’Or to peddle an academy kid.

There’s less ambiguity in the wisdom of what Barat has done there. It reeks. It carries the stench of an agent who evidently doesn’t mind so much if the labels attached to Gabriel today stick for the remainder of his career.

Earlier this month, his handlers felt it prudent to place him in an interview with the Madrid-based newspaper Marca and Gabriel said: ‘My dream is to win a Ballon d'Or’

Gabriel's representative Ali Barat, who is 30 years older than his client and saw no harm in a video that invoked the Ballon d’Or to peddle an academy kid

I can remember when Mauricio Pochettino once made the blunder of placing Marcus Edwards, a Tottenham wonderkid, into the same sentence as Lionel Messi. His point was that he had some similar movement patterns, but the fact the lad was named mini-Messi in training didn’t help – it was a tag that endured.

Thankfully, Edwards has carved out a respectable career at Burnley via Sporting in Portugal, but Pochettino regretted the words as soon as they left his mouth.

That’s different to designing and releasing a video, of course. That’s different to a process involving some level of sign-off. That’s different to the grubby act of hyping a very young guy to a standard reached by only five Englishmen in history.

A question at this stage: where was Gabriel’s family when this was being decided? That’s somewhat loaded because there is chatter about how much of the United separation has been driven by Gabriel’s father, Joe O'Cearuill, formerly a professional himself for Brighton, Barnet and the Republic of Ireland.

I’d add that many of those noises have originated from within Carrington. It might simply be the bitter discourse of the jilted. But a recurring sentiment among some United staffers is that the father became difficult during the breakdown in relations.

These are lines we have heard before in football. But for once, United do not appear to have done much wrong. There was genuine care for the player. And if there is one thing they can guarantee, it is that young talents get a good chance, though evidently not enough to please Gabriel’s camp.

A demand for minutes against Azerbaijani side Sabah in the Champions League was a bad look; similar might be said with less force around reports that he changed his name from Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill for commercial reasons, feeding one of those blurry conversations about where the athlete ends and the product begins.

Gabriel’s early days with Epic and Barat and his content wing do not serve much encouragement on that front.

Gabriel's father Joe O'Cearuill was briefly in Arsenal's reserves before going on to play for Brighton, Barnet and the Republic of Ireland

United do not appear to have done much wrong. There was genuine care for the player. And if there is one thing they can guarantee, it is that young talents get a good chance

It is worth stating that the teenager at the heart of it all is not considered to be a bad sort. Far from it.

None of his ascent was accompanied by the worrying noises that followed another prodigy in Ravel Morrison – once described by Sir Alex Ferguson as having 'as much natural talent as any youngster we ever signed', but who made all of three League Cup appearances for United before a journeyman career through the Championship, Italy, Mexico, Sweden, the Netherlands, the US and the UAE.

One source has suggested Gabriel even cried when he said his goodbyes back in September.

It might be over-reaching to claim he has left the club against his own better judgment, but there is no doubt he has gambled hugely on Real Madrid.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is pretty handy and has found it tough there; Martin Odegaard is a far closer parallel to Gabriel having moved to Madrid aged 15, and he played 11 games in three seasons.

If the pathway was blocked at United, then what is it at a club who employ Vinicius Junior, Rodrygo, Yan Diomande, Arda Guler, Endrick, Brahim Diaz, Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe in Gabriel's positions?

A new language and surroundings are large hurdles for a young player, especially one whose ambitions are so public and grand. It won’t be a quiet arrival by any definition, even those found in the quirky dictionary of Ali Barat, and the pressure will be significant.

Hopefully such factors don’t impact upon an exciting trajectory. That would be an epic shame.

If United's pathway was blocked, then what is it at a club with (L-R) Vinicius Junior, Jude Bellingham, Rodrygo, Kylian Mbappe and plenty more in Gabriel's positions?

A new language and surroundings are large hurdles for a young player, and hopefully such factors don’t impact upon an exciting trajectory. That would be an epic shame

Welsh Rugby Union's 20,000 reasons to be ashamed

Among the joys of this job is being present at rare moments of sporting greatness. The Welsh win over the All Blacks last weekend was one such occasion and, for me, it was compounded by a subsequent email from a lovely chap named John Evans, aged 87 and from Tredegar in Blaenau Gwent.

John had watched the game on television, but was part of what must be a dwindling group who could say they were there the last time Wales had beaten New Zealand, at the Arms Park in 1953.

After detailing how he, ‘a small-bottomed outside-half’, had left himself with no view of the pitch at the back of the stand, John went on to recall that the crowd around him and a friend ‘decided to pass us over everyone’s head back down to the front’. He landed just in time to see Ken Jones score the winning try. His excitement in sharing a memory from 73 years ago was spelled out in block capitals.

One of the consequences of the ongoing shambles at the Welsh Rugby Union is that there were 20,000 empty seats at the Principality Stadium last weekend, mainly due to a combination of apathy and protest. Accordingly, there will be 20,000 fewer people with a great story to tell decades from now. While the WRU ponder their next blunders, they might wish to consider some of the above.

The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

#1053. How AI shocks are rattling the next generation of mathematicians — in charts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Many early-career mathematicians are concerned about how AI models will affect their career prospects.Credit: Getty

AI company Anthropic has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most famous open problem in mathematics — with the help of its model Claude. The proposed proof, which is still being scrutinized, is the latest in a series of spectacular artificial-intelligence advances in mathematics that are upending the field.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

But the technology’s rapid progress is making early-career mathematicians anxious about the impact that it will have on their futures, according to two studies released in October.

One was a survey of graduate students and postdocs1 designed by three PhD students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge and uploaded to the preprint server arXiv. The other was conducted by the Martingale Foundation, a non-profit organization in London that supports postgraduate students. It surveyed people at all career stages, but the respondents were limited to UK mathematicians.

Key concerns included job security and feelings of demotivation — 70% of respondents to the student-led survey said that they were now more likely to consider careers outside academia.

Many mathematicians interviewed by Nature say that the survey results match what they have been hearing from their peers. Graduate students, in particular, feel that they need to develop their own skills and prove their worth at solving mathematical problems without AI. Some are also concerned about the long-term availability of academic jobs — and whether hard-won results produced by their human reasoning could be put them at a disadvantage in a job market in which others use AI.

Source: Martindale Foundation report Mathematics in the Age of AI: The Impact on Postgraduate Experience

“The younger generation seems much more sceptical,” says Tasmin Chu, a mathematics PhD student at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. “Fundamentally, that’s because they are in a much worse material position.”

The student-led survey found that only around 7% of the 268 voluntary respondents — most of whom were at US institutions — felt that AI developments would make it easier for them to get a job that would lead to an eventual professorship. Meanwhile, more than 75% of people expected it to become harder.

Only 13% of respondents said that they were letting AI tools produce papers for them from start to finish, although a majority of people said that they were using the tools for literature searches or finding mistakes in their papers. Of those respondents who do use AI tools, more than half said that they dislike doing so, and only around 30% said that they enjoy using them. More than three-quarters of respondents said that they would be unhappy if an AI model were to solve a problem that they had worked on (see ‘Pride in discovery’).

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03795-5

Brandenberger, A., Mularczyk, H. & Woodruff, D. Preprint at arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.40584 (2026).

#1051. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.
