#970. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

#969. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

#968. ‘Mozart of maths’ Terence Tao is your guide to what underpins reality

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Itai Yanai is a professor in the Institute for Systems Genetics, New York University Grossman School of Medicine, New York City.

After centuries of debate, a mathematical proof of the most efficient way to stack balls was produced only in 1998. Credit: Getty

Six Maths Essentials: How to Model the World Terence Tao Pelican

Can knowing about central principles in mathematics help us to understand our world? Leading mathematician Terence Tao — who has been called the Mozart of maths — explains how it can in his latest book, Six Maths Essentials.

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world

For Tao, the six concepts are the building blocks of reality that together provide an opportunity to better understand it. They are, he writes: “numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking, algebra as the gateway to abstraction, geometry as a way to go beyond what we can see, probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking, analysis as a means to tame the very large or very small, and dynamics as the mathematics of change”.

Each is described with elegant minimalism, consistent with Tao’s vocation of writing concise mathematical proofs. In its brevity, the book evokes physicist Richard Feynman’s Six Easy Pieces (1994), which explains fundamental physics concepts to the layperson. Similarly, the beauty of Tao’s book is seeing maths through his eyes, describing its spirit as well as generalizing across the discipline.

For instance, Tao describes how artificial intelligence inspires awe and magic — it easily lives up to science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke’s famous statement that “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic”. But AI has a dark side, too. It can lead us to become superstitious and think that the tool cares about us, or to develop a sense of fear that we wouldn’t know how to live if it malfunctioned.

Tao makes the case that maths has played an important part in the story of humanity. We meet famous mathematicians such as ninth-century Islamic astronomer Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī, who pioneered algebra, following in the footsteps of the ancient Babylonians, and gave his name to the Latin form of the term algorithm. Others solved real-world problems, from calculating the distance between Earth and the Sun to understanding the 2008 global financial crisis.

We learn about mathematicians who overcame the desire of philosophers such as Immanuel Kant to pigeonhole geometry into a single ‘true’ concept, instead finding that there is a plurality of connected geometries. Other mathematicians revealed the laws of chance through their passion for gambling.

AI has transformed maths — this is how we got here

AI has transformed maths — this is how we got here

Tao invokes hardly any equations, opting instead for intuitive explanations. It is through this same intuition, Tao argues, that children work out that there is no highest number, thus deducing the concept of infinity. He discusses the elegance of algebra and its ability to solve many problems without requiring a tailored equation for each application. This generalizability, he notes, is what distinguishes maths from organic chemistry — which was his least favourite subject in school, he writes, because it required memorizing disparate facts without organizing principles like those found in maths.

He is at his best explaining difficult topics to the public. On analysis, he writes that there are both hard and soft aspects, corresponding to quantitative and qualitative modes. He calls analysis the accountant of maths: “auditing and proving which techniques work under what circumstances”.

He uses mathematician John Conway’s Game of Life to demonstrate the need to study dynamics. In this game, simple rules are applied to a matrix of elements that are either ‘on’ or ‘off’ as they unfold into complex patterns. The grid functions as a rudimentary yet, in principle, fully functional computer.

John Conway used games to transform mathematics.Credit: Dith Pran/NYT/Redux/eyevine

Importantly, Tao conveys how mathematicians think as they discover new maths. He distinguishes the ‘cold’ maths found in textbooks from the active maths that happens as mathematicians explore fresh domains. For example, he describes how Carl Friedrich Gauss imagined what it would be like to be on the surface of a sphere — a view that led to his “remarkable theorem” on the properties of curvature, proved in 1827.

#967. Jude Bellingham scores 'the best goal of my life' as his stunning long-range volley helps Real Madrid come from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in the Champions League

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 18:45 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 19:32 EST, 24 November 2026

Jude Bellingham underlined his class once more with a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

With Real trailing 1-0 at half-time, the England superstar - who started as a substitute to rest - was one of three changes made by Jose Mourinho and his impact was felt 15 minutes later in an emphatic style.

Collecting a loose ball from around 25 yards outside the box, Bellingham controlled it with his left foot, before flicking it up with his right foot and volleying it with the outside of that boot into the far corner of the PSV goal. The pace and precision of the strike was breathtaking as it flew past Matej Kovar and hit the inside of the post before going in.

It was a strike that was befitting of any match, and it proved to be the decisive one as that made it 2-1 to the hosts before they later ran riot.

Speaking post-match, Bellingham was clear where he ranked that finish, declaring: 'I think this was the best goal of my life.'

He later elaborated to TNT Sports about his goal: 'They're [his goals] normally a lot closer, aren't they,' he joked.

SENSATIONAL JUDE BELLINGHAM 🤯Bellingham gives the hosts the lead with a magnificent volley 🔥 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/WdP6ULx8wE

Jude Bellingham (right) scored a stunning volley to inspire Real Madrid to beat PSV Eindhoven

Bellingham came off the bench to put Real ahead with this beautiful right-footed volley

PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar could only watch on as the ball flew past him and go into the net

'That one was a nice one, it popped up for me nicely and I just thought I'd hit it with the outside of my boot.

'I'm not one for smashing the ball too hard and it was a nice moment and important for the win as well.'

Bellingham's performance, he also set up Vinicius Jr for the fifth goal, was acknowledged by Mourinho and Real captain Fede Valverde, who scored their equaliser, post-match too.

'Obviously Jude is a different type of player and he gave us what we didn't have in the first half,' Mourinho said. 'He changed the game, scored an incredible goal.'

Valverde concurred declaring: 'He did well. We were struggling to keep the ball behind their midfielders and when Jude came in he gave us that tranquillity to control possession.'

The strike comes a day after Daily Mail Sport reported that the 23-year-old is in advance talks over a new Real Madrid contract that will make him one of the best-paid players in Europe.

Madrid have been eager to tie down the in-form England midfielder beyond his current contract, understood to be worth around £12.5million a year after tax, which runs until 2029, in recognition of his performances.

Talks were initiated in September over an extension until 2031 and have been progressing well since with sources at Madrid confident they are close to reaching a conclusion.

Bellingham is in advance contract talks with Real Madrid over signing an extension until 2031

Bellingham is expected to be handed improved terms to put him on par with team-mate Vinicius Jr, who agreed a new deal last summer reputedly on around £500,000 a week after tax.

As for Tuesday's win over PSV, Real are now top of the Champions League league phase standings after maintaining their 100 per cent record in the competition this season with a fifth-straight win.

1. Erling Haaland, Manchester City: £510,000 per week

2. Kylian Mbappe, Real Madrid: £503,000 per week

3. Vinicius Jr, Real Madrid: £500,000 per week

4. Harry Kane, Bayern Munich: £402,000 per week

5. Virgil van Dijk, Liverpool: £350,000 per week

However, they didn't have it all their own way as PSV took a deserved lead in the 32nd minute from the penalty spot, with 37-year-old captain Ivan Perisic showing all his experience, ignoring the whistles ringing out around the Bernabeu before sending Thibaut Courtois the wrong way.

They almost doubled their lead before the break as the unmarked Kodai Sano glanced a header off target as the visitors continued to cause Real serious problems.

Real equalised five minutes after the break, thanks to Arda Guler's quick-thinking, with the Turkish midfielder flicking a backheeled pass to Valverde in the area, who steered his first-time shot into the bottom corner.

Real's fans were on their feet 10 minutes later, scarcely believing what they had seen, while Bellingham's team-mates looked similarly shell-shocked.

Marc Cucurella walked away with his head in his hands in wonder while the other Real players rushed to congratulate the scorer.

Real took command after Bellingham's goal and punished a loose pass in the PSV defence, Guler finding the unmarked Mbappe to extend the France forward's scoring run to seven successive Champions League appearances.

Mbappe added his second before Vinicius rounded off a resounding victory from Bellingham's pass, underlining the Spanish side's credentials as serious contenders to take Paris Saint-Germain's crown.

#965. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

#964. Man United FURIOUS with Howard Webb after he backed decision to send off Leny Yoro at Anfield: Club to take fight to Premier League as red card is OVERTURNED after appeal

Published: 10:23 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 02:10 EST, 25 November 2026

Manchester United have hit out at referees’ boss Howard Webb after winning an appeal to have Leny Yoro’s red card at Liverpool overturned.

An FA independent regulatory commission on Tuesday ruled that Yoro was wrongfully dismissed by referee Sam Barrott at Anfield on Sunday as United’s 10 men suffered a 4-0 defeat in Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge.

But United are furious that Pro Ref boss Webb has refused to admit the error after he backed Barrott’s decision and VAR’s refusal to overturn it on the Mic’d Up show on Sky Sports. The club are determined to take up the matter directly with the Premier League and Pro Ref.

Yoro was sent off for pushing Alexander Isak in the back, but United disputed the referee’s view that the Liverpool striker would have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

The FA panel appeared to agree as it rescinded Yoro’s red card and lifted his one-match ban on the basis that he did not deny Isak an obvious goalscoring opportunity – meaning the Frenchman can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

However, Webb argued: ‘That was the referee’s call, made on the field. Then the VAR checks whether the decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect – and formed the opinion it wasn’t.

Leny Yoro has seen his red card suspension overturned following an appeal by Man United

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb believed it was the right decision for Yoro to be sent off on Sunday

‘I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong.’

United sources have branded this interpretation as ‘totally wrong’ and say it is a process error that fails to interpret the rules properly. They believe that the VAR audio proves there was no meaningful consideration given to challenging Barrott’s decision.

United dispute that it was subjective call and say that it can be proved objectively in a matter of minutes using data that Isak could not have reached the ball before Lammens, even at top speed.

Pochettino blamed the decision for United’s defeat at Anfield, and took aim at VAR again after landing in Portugal last night (tues) for the Champions League tie against Sporting Lisbon.

‘I’m very disappointed because I think this kind of thing never can happen,’ said Pochettino, who also felt that Dominik Szoboszlai’s opening goal from the resulting free kick should have been disallowed because Bradley Barcola made contact with United’s defensive wall.

‘The referee can make a mistake but if we have VAR what were they doing? We need to take time to review the situation.’

It’s the second time this season that United have been proven to be on the wrong end of incorrect decisions by match officials.

In September, Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland’s winning goal for Manchester City in the Old Trafford derby was allowed to stand.

Tonight’s (wed) game sees United captain Bruno Fernandes face his old team Sporting amid increasing uncertainty over his future at Old Trafford after talks over a new contact stalled.

‘We have time to speak about that,’ said Fernandes. ‘I know it's my future and I probably shouldn't look that way because I haven't got long left, but I'm more worried about results.’

Asked if he would consider a return to Sporting, who sold him to United for £68million in 2020, Fernandes added: ‘I will never close the door to Sporting. It will always be a club with a special place in my heart.’

#959. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

#958. Build for the future climate — or waste trillions of dollars

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Saroj Kanta Mishra is a professor and leads the Department of Science and Technology Centre of Excellence for Climate Information at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Delhi, India.

Reservoirs need to be constructed in ways that help to avoid water shortages as heatwaves increase. Credit: Ander Gillenea/AFP via Getty

“Prepare for El Niño”, the World Meteorological Organization warned earlier this year. Governments are responding by adjusting agricultural practices and securing water supplies. But climate measures should not begin when a hazardous event approaches, they should be part of a wider strategy of planning for a warmer future.

Repeated disasters cause immense disruption to people’s lives and livelihoods, and the economic loss and damage can add up to trillions of dollars. Climate warnings and actions taken in anticipation of disasters can help to reduce the impact on people and economies. But their effectiveness is constrained by existing limitations, such as a community’s access to resources and infrastructure.

Such vulnerabilities must be addressed at their source, when decisions about development and infrastructure are being made, so that climate risks are reduced through better planning rather than through reactive responses to individual events. Decisions about the location and capacity of reservoirs, agricultural drainage systems and the design of cities and transport infrastructure, for instance, cannot be changed easily once they have been made.

Much of what is being built now will shape societies for decades. To meet global climate and development objectives by 2030, nearly US$7 trillion of infrastructure investment is needed annually1. Global annual infrastructure spending is projected to increase from $4.4 trillion in 2024 to $6.9 trillion by 20502. But it will be wasted if projects are designed inadequately for the climate conditions that people will face.

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

The super El Niño is more than a climate shock — it’s a health one, too

Decisions for development projects are being hampered because climate projections are often not integrated into planning processes. Another challenge is the limited availability of reliable, decision-relevant climate information for the 5–30-year period — an intermediate timescale between seasonal forecasts and long-term climate projections that is particularly relevant for planning major infrastructure such as roads and reservoirs3.

Climate services can provide this information. Scientists can improve climate projections. Development planners can assess projects. But unless these functions are connected within the development process, the system as a whole remains reactive.

A common operating system would change that. Government ministries that oversee development would determine which planning decisions need to consider climate information. Planning institutions would ensure that climate assessments are undertaken and considered as part of investment approval for climate-sensitive projects. Climate agencies would provide the scientific information, which would improve both planning and science. Here, I outline how such a system would work.

A central government planning institution should establish a small climate-planning unit within it, not separately. Corresponding units could be set up in state or subnational planning institutions when appropriate. In countries without central planning institutions, the same functions could be assigned to existing government institutions.

The central unit would set common standards, consolidate information needs across sectors and jurisdictions, coordinate with national climate agencies and ensure that climate considerations are incorporated into the planning and appraisal of projects of national significance. Subnational units would apply the framework to local projects and feed emerging requirements back to the central unit.

Responsibilities should be made explicit. Ministries should identify the climate information needed to support various sectors. Planning institutions would coordinate those needs and ensure that such climate information informs investment decisions. Climate agencies would produce the underlying scientific information and ensure its technical accuracy and quality.

This division matters. The proposal is not to make development planners become climate scientists, nor to make climate agencies become development authorities. It is to give them a permanent institutional connection.

The rules governing public investment in development should be changed to follow this principle: funding for a major climate-sensitive project should not be approved without a demonstration that it has been designed for the climate it is expected to face.

Governments should request climate assessments for large, long-lived and climate-sensitive projects before approving funds. Assessments should be provided early enough in the process to influence the location, technology, scale and design of a project. For a new reservoir, for example, the relevant planning unit would identify the climate conditions that the reservoir is likely to face during its operational lifetime, with implications for where and how it is built.

A climate-planning unit would not decide whether the project should proceed; it would certify that the relevant climate risks have been assessed and that reasonable alternatives have been considered. Its assessment would be considered as part of an investment appraisal alongside economic, technical, social and environmental factors.

To be effective, the system must connect three functions: development demand, climate analysis and investment approval.

Ministries should periodically identify the climate information needed for their forthcoming development decisions. The central planning unit should consolidate these requests and work with climate agencies to determine what information can be provided, what projects require fresh analysis and when investment for climate observations, modelling or scientific capacity is needed.

Kenya’s government is implementing measures to reduce flooding from rivers.Credit: James Wakibia/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty

This comprehensive approach would provide climate scientists with clear directives from the development system. It would encourage them to improve climate projections for specific regions, over a 5–30-year typical planning horizon, and for distinct sectors. It would also reduce the need for individual development projects to commission their own climate analyses, which can be patchy and inconsistent.

An analysis of six generations of assessment reports from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found, for instance, that inconsistent climate projections across many low- and middle-income countries were complicating adaptation and long-term planning efforts4. For example, in some regions, precipitation was projected by one assessment to increase, and by the next to decrease, with successive views bouncing back and forth.

Such disagreements undermine a region’s ability to make long-term investments. They increase the likelihood of costly misallocation of funds, maladaptation to climate risks and infrastructure being developed that is ill-suited to future climate conditions. Dams, cities and transport corridors cannot be easily redesigned or rebuilt once constructed.

This challenge is compounded by the fact that climate models perform poorly across many climate-vulnerable regions. In South Asia, for example, simulations of temperature and precipitation can differ from observed values by as much as 25% and 100%, respectively5. Such biases limit the reliability of model-based climate information for guiding long-term development decisions.

That’s why the proposed climate-informed planning units would ensure that climate agencies’ work is guided by clearly articulated development needs and that the information they provide is reliable and fit for development planning. Importantly, they would not be a replacement for other climate services, which can remain focused on providing accurate information for a wide range of sectors6,7. The aim is to bridge a specific gap between climate information and development.

A climate assessment for a development project should not become obsolete as soon as the work is approved. Both central and subnational planning units should regularly monitor whether new climate observations or scientific assessments change the climate risks identified. If they do, an updated assessment should be returned to the planning authority.

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming

The units should evaluate whether the climate information generated by the system is useful. Regular technical reviews would compare climate projections with observations and assess whether the information remains fit for planning purposes. Institutional reviews conducted by climate-planning units could also examine whether big projects have incorporated climate foresight and whether it influenced their designs.

These reviews would create a feedback loop. Development decisions would determine what information is needed, which could be satisfied by climate-science and investment-appraisal processes. Data from implemented projects would then be fed back into the system to update climate information and plans going forwards.

#957. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

#955. Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

#953. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”

England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. It took us a while to grow into the game but after 15 minutes I think we did OK, got the goal and got better and more confident and had some good actions and good chances, good half-chances.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. It was like our third goal was coming and we had some easy ball losses in our own half that killed our momentum.

“An awkward moment in our box can always happen. It’s important to react and we did it.”

On his defenders: “Good. It was demanding for Dan Burn and also for Jarell [Quansah] because they [Croatia] play with a back five and have two number 10s in between the lines.

“It was a lot of work to do, a lot of communication but they did very well.”

On what will be better against Spain on Sunday: “I don’t know. Everything will be different. Completely different scenario, completely different setup, but I’m very positive that we will get what we want.”

England put in an the-Lord-Mayor’s-show performance following their 7-0 victory over Croatia. But it was still good enough to beat the same opponents 2-1 on the night Harry Kane celebrated his 126th record-breaking cap at Wembley.

Kane capped the night with the winning goal from the penalty spot, but a poor second-half showing – after Morgan Rogers had opened the scoring in the 24th minute – allowed Petar Sucic to equalise, aided by a dreadful mistake by Jarell Quansah.

England captain Harry Kane, speaking to ITV: “An incredible gesture, reception at the start of the game. Once the game starts, it’s about getting the win, getting the three points. We’re playing against a tough team, a team that wanted to prove something tonight.

“I think for large spells of the game we done well. Got a little bit tired towards the end but overall a really great win and sets up a great game on Sunday now.”

On how he was feeling as he stepped up for his penalty: “Same as ever. I missed my last one for Bayern, so I think it’s always important to try and bounce back with the next one. Try to not miss two in a row but executing. I practised yesterday like I always do and it’s just about going out there and doing it out on the pitch.

“I think we gave away a few too many easy balls, especially in our own half, which killed the momentum a little bit. I think we had enough chances to score two or three but we’re playing against a good team.

“We’re in the midst of a run of tough games for club and country, so you can’t always expect things to be perfect. Of course, we know we can improve on a few bits and we will need to if we want to win on Sunday, but ultimately it’s about getting a win tonight.”

On aiming to beat Spain and top the group: “100%. After the first game when we lost here against them, we knew we left a bit out there. We knew we could’ve done a bit better. We said to ourselves let’s win every game until the next one and see what happens. It’s the perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves.”

Thomas Tuchel tells ITV: “A good win, we wanted this desperately, we deserved it. It was hard work against a good opponent.” We will bring you more from the England head coach shortly.

Harry Kane has told ITV that it was an “incredible reception” for him at the start of a “really good win”. We will bring you the captain’s full quotes shortly.

While top spot in the group is still up for grabs, England have booked their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, which will take place in March 2027.

The winners of those ties progress to the Nations League Finals in June.

Harry Kane has now scored 92 goals in 126 appearances for England.

Thomas Tuchel has said he has “unfinished business” with England and will remain in his position for the Euros in 2028, but did say that he would return to club football after seeing out his contract.

“I signed the contract, I want to stay until the Euros,” he said this week. “I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

But he added: “I miss the 50 matches [a season].

“I miss the two minutes when everything is done. You go out two minutes before the whistle goes, it’s like the best two minutes, everything is done and you’re in a full stadium, lights are on and you’re just so excited and you’re part of it.”

Shortly before kick-off, Croatia captain Luka Modric will present England captain Harry Kane with a special gift from the Croatian Football Federation (HNS), marking his Ballon d’Or win and his achievement in becoming England’s all-time record appearance holder with 126 caps.

Modric is not in the starting line-up but the 41-year-old has 206 caps for his country and will present Kane with a specially crafted replica of the first football ever brought to Croatia, which English industrialists introduced to the town of Zupanja in 1880. This event is regarded as the beginning of organised football on Croatian soil.

England’s 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic last month left them on nine points after four Nations League group games.

It came after a 2-0 win in the away contest, a 7-0 thumping of Croatia and a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

A draw tonight will be enough for Thomas Tuchel’s side to book their place in the quarter-finals of the competition.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

The two worst sides to finish bottom are automatically relegated, while the other bottom sides and third-placed sides are at risk of relegation via a play-off.

Few expect Jobe to be better than his older brother. While Jobe will make his England debut just two months after turning 21, Jude’s first cap came aged 17. By the time that he was Jobe’s age now, Jude had already thrived for England in two international tournaments. But Jobe has one major sporting advantage: he is the younger sibling.

Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the FA’s England app as he discussed his call-up.

“It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great. To be called up for England is a dream itself and I’ve been so proud to have the opportunity to represent England at every age group.

“I always enjoyed coming away with England, I love competing against top players at whichever age group. But to have that chance of an opportunity to represent England with my brother, it’s really hard to put into words.

“I don’t have the words, really. I think it’s only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you’ll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family.”

There will be a special pre-match presentation to honour Harry Kane becoming England’s record appearance maker, with 126 caps, overtaking Peter Shilton. Shilton has held the record since 1989.

The goalkeeper is at Wembley to formally mark Kane’s achievement. The England captain will also show the Ballon d’Or trophy he won last month.

Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph from last month will also be celebrated tonight before kick-off, along with his record appearance.

“I think I maybe underappreciated how big it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“It’s just been crazy, whether it’s messages on my phone or on social media, or people calling me, and just being in the street and everyone congratulating me.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually said my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Thomas Tuchel has said Harry Kane was the deserved winner of the Ballon d’Or, with the England head coach describing the striker as “an extraordinary player”.

“He wins the Ballon d’Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches,” Tuchel said when announcing the latest squad.

“Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player.”

Kane said: “It’s not about me – it’s about the team. I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

Harry Kane starts for England in what will be a record 126th appearance for his country.

Thomas Tuchel makes three changes from last month’s win over Czech Republic, with Dan Burn, Declan Rice and Anthony Gordon replacing Marc Guehi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Eberechi Eze.

Harry Kane will become England’s record appearance maker this evening, with the 33-year-old set to earn his 126th cap.

The striker started his international career against Lithuania in March 2015, scoring just 79 second after replacing Wayne Rooney at Wembley.

Eight years later, Kane surpassed Rooney as the country’s record goalscorer, netting his 54th England goal in an away contest with Italy.

He equalled Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps last month against Czech Republic as he scored his 90th and 91st international goals.

England will be hoping for a repeat of their fixture against Croatia last month, with Thomas Tuchel’s side producing an emphatic 7-0 victory in Rijeka.

England were 4-0 up at half-time of the Nations League contest, which was attended by 6,000 schoolchildren and 100 visiting fans, with Croatia supporters sanctioned over previous bad behaviour.

England’s front four of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka were all on the scoresheet in the opening period, with Kane and Saka doubling their tallies in the second half before a late seventh from Morgan Rogers.

The last time we met Croatia in the Nations League 👊 https://t.co/b07QcUSlPI

Good evening and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of England vs Croatia in the Nations League, with the hosts’ captain Harry Kane set to become the country’s most-capped player.

The 33-year-old has enjoyed a memorable few weeks, becoming the first English Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years and following it up with a new Bayern Munich contract, and an appearance at Wembley tonight will take him clear of Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane scored twice in his record-equalling appearance against Czech Republic at Wembley last month, extending his international tally to 91 goals – a total that is unrivalled for England.

“It’s not about me – it’s about the team,” Kane said before tonight’s landmark moment. “I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

The 3-0 home victory over Czech Republic left England on nine points after four Nations League group games, with a 2-0 win in the away contest and a 7-0 thumping of Croatia coming after a 3-2 defeat against world champions Spain.

Thomas Tuchel will be hoping that his side can inflict another heavy defeat on Croatia this evening, but a draw will be enough to book their place in the quarter-finals, with the group’s top two teams progressing.

While Kane will collect plaudits for his 126th cap, attention will also be on a potential first, with Jude Bellingham’s younger brother, Jobe, included in a senior England squad for the first time.

The two Bellinghams appearing together in a senior match would be a new experience for them, while it would be the first time that brothers have taken to the field together for England in 19 years.

“I can’t ignore it, but obviously with Jude being here too, it’s a great, great feeling for the family,” Jobe said on the Football Association’s England app. “It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great.”

#952. Architecture of the poxvirus early-transcription machinery and portal complex

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1–3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.
